newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe faces tough sales pitch on jobs.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe faces tough sales pitch on jobs.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, dogged by near-record unemployment, faces an uphill task selling his latest proposals to foster jobs for the young on Monday before an audience of union heads, businessmen and associations.
The conference at Juppe's Matignon offices is certain to rekindle controversy over labour flexibility which is the focus of several strikes and protests in various sectors.
It will launch a week of key data on consumer confidence and prospects for economic growth, including a forecast by the rich nations' OECD club on Thursday.

"Youth unemployment was stabilised in 1996. Obviously this result is far short of our ambitions. We must mobilise all partners," Juppe told the daily Liberation in an interview to be published on Monday.
President Jacques Chirac has made employment for young people his main theme to woo voters in the run-up to general elections due by early next year.

The powerful bosses' CNPF federation will push for more flexible work contracts while several trade unions will demand the opposite. Unions suspect the bosses of trying to buy low-cost labour with a suggested scheme called "first professional experience".
The plan initially provided for nine-month stints in companies with payment of up to 1,700 francs ($340), but the CNPF agreed to shorten it to the length of a university term, some 4-1/2 months.
"There is no question of it lasting more than a term," said Frederic Hocquard of the students' Unef-ID union, adding that bosses should not confuse work experience with a first job.
The unemployment rate is close to 25 percent among those under 25 years old, against 12.7 percent for the working-age population as a whole.

Juppe said he was against the idea of a minimum wage specifically for young people "especially given the fact that there are many different formulas which cut the cost of labour for companies". Apprenticeships and the new work experience scheme must be a priority, he said.

France's biggest union, the pro-Socialist CFDT, said it was ready to discuss with other unions and with the centre-right government plans for early retirement off-set by the hiring of young people, or a cut in working hours.
Juppe also said he wanted to ensure more young people to get a first work experience abroad. "There aren't enough French people abroad. That's a bother, because the markets are over there," he added.
President Jacques Chirac, who has said he wants to make 1997 the year of jobs for the young, has urged them "not to be scared of expatriating themselves".

"That's an amazing acknowledgement of political impotence," retorted Regis Juanico, president of the Young Socialists' Movement. He said Monday's conference "is a publicity stunt to try and re-conquer the votes of young people."
